# Introduction

::: {.callout-note title="Add to tutorial"}
Resources on boosting come in two kinds. Textbooks such as Hastie et al. [-@hastie2009] derive the algorithms mathematically, without code. Applied guides such as Boehmke and Greenwell [-@boehmke2019] and tutorials such as Pargent et al. [-@pargent2023] show how to call the implementations, without opening them. Kunapuli [-@kunapuli2023] builds the algorithms by hand, but in Python, for a general audience, and on toy data. This tutorial fills the gap between the two kinds for psychologists: it builds AdaBoost step by step in R, on a question from their own field, checks the result against a package, and evaluates it project by project, as the data demand. Pargent et al. [-@pargent2023] teach the machine-learning workflow; this tutorial opens the algorithm. Readers need both.
:::

# Empirical Example

#### Listing 2

Code to load the dataset.

```{r listing-2}
# Load data
data(altmext)
```

::: {.callout-note title="Add to tutorial"}
The dataset integrates 202 study effects from seven replication projects. Each row is one effect from an original study, paired with the outcome of its replication; Altmejd et al. [-@altmejd2019] call these study-replication pairs.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Check in tutorial"}
Use "study effects" for the rows throughout. Two places to align in `adatutorial.tex`:

- Module 2 calls them "studies" (e.g., "all studies with a power of less than 0.9305", ll. 817--905, and the comments of Listing 11).
- "Observations" means two things: the original sample size (`n.o`, "the number of observations", ll. 281, 825, 840, 858) and the data points that AdaBoost weights ("observation weights"). Keep "observations" for the weights and say "sample size" for `n.o`.
:::

::: {.callout-important title="Changed since submission"}
- `altmext` (seven projects, 202 study effects) instead of `altmejd`.
:::

#### Listing 3

Code to prepare the data.

```{r listing-3}
# Reviewer metrics (names)
pred_nms <- c("power.o", "effect_size.o", "n.o", "p_value.o")

# Outcome variable (name)
out_nme <- "replicate"

# Variables of interest (names)
voi_nms <- c(pred_nms, out_nme)

# Shorten 'altmext'
df <- altmext
```

::: {.callout-important title="Changed since submission"}

# Module 1: Data Splitting

#### Listing 4

Code to do a 70/30 simple random split.

```{r listing-4}
# For reproducibility
set.seed(112)

# Split proportion
prop_train <- 0.7

# Number of effects
n_fx <- nrow(df)

# Number of training samples
n_train <- round(n_fx * prop_train)

# Row positions
fx_seq <- seq_len(n_fx)

# Sample from sequence
fx_smpl <- sample(fx_seq, n_train)

# Inclusion indicator
train_ind <- fx_seq %in% fx_smpl

# Training set
train <- df[train_ind, ]

# Test set (the rest)
test <- df[!train_ind, ]
```

::: {.callout-important title="Changed since submission"}
- A logical inclusion indicator (`train_ind`) instead of negative indexing (`train_idx`).
- `prop_train` instead of `prop`.
- The rest is the test set (`test`), not `testvalid`.
:::

#### Listing 5

Code to do a 70/15/15 simple random split in one pass.

```{r listing-5}
# For reproducibility
set.seed(112)

# Split proportions (of all effects)
prop <- c(train = 0.7, valid = 0.15, test = 0.15)

# Set sizes
n <- round(n_fx * prop)

# Training sample and inclusion indicator
train_smpl <- sample(fx_seq, n[["train"]])
train_ind <- fx_seq %in% train_smpl

# Validation sample and inclusion indicator
valid_smpl <- sample(fx_seq[!train_ind], n[["valid"]])
valid_ind <- fx_seq %in% valid_smpl

# Training set
train <- df[train_ind, ]

# Validation set
valid <- df[valid_ind, ]

# Test set (the rest)
test <- df[!train_ind & !valid_ind, ]
```

::: {.callout-note title="Add to tutorial"}
All three proportions refer to the whole dataset, so `0.15` means 15% of all 202 study effects.
:::

::: {.callout-important title="Changed since submission"}
- One pass with `prop <- c(train = 0.7, valid = 0.15, test = 0.15)`, instead of a second step with `prop <- 0.5` on `testvalid` (15 percent of the whole is half of the remaining 30 percent).
:::

#### Listing 6

Code to check for imbalances in the outcome variable of the original dataset
and the held-out set.

```{r listing-6}
# Frequency tables
tbl_orig <- table(df$replicate)
tbl_out <- table(df$replicate[!train_ind])

# Relative frequencies
proportions(tbl_orig)
proportions(tbl_out)
```

::: {.callout-important title="Changed since submission"}
- The held-out set via `!train_ind` (`tbl_out`), instead of `testvalid` (`tbl_testvalid`).
:::

#### Listing 7

Code to do a 70/30 stratified split.

```{r listing-7}
# For reproducibility
set.seed(112)

# Split proportion
prop_train <- 0.7

# Partition data based on outcome
set_split <- split(df, df$replicate)

# Number of training samples per stratum
n_train <- lapply(set_split, \(set) round(nrow(set) * prop_train))

# Training sample per stratum
train_smpl <- mapply(\(set, n) sample(set$eid, n), set_split, n_train)

# Inclusion indicator
train_ind <- df$eid %in% unlist(train_smpl)

# Combined sets
strat_diy <- list(train = df[train_ind, ], test = df[!train_ind, ])
```

::: {.callout-note title="Add to tutorial"}
`\(set)` is R's shorthand for `function(set)`.
:::

::: {.callout-important title="Changed since submission"}
- Lambdas (`\(set)`) instead of `function(set)`, and `set$eid` instead of `set[, "eid"]`.
- `train_smpl` and `train_ind` instead of `strat_idx` and `train_idx`.
- Returns the list `strat_diy` (train, test) instead of `train` and `testvalid`.
:::

#### Listing 8

Code to do a 70/15/15 stratified split.

```{r listing-8}
# For reproducibility
set.seed(112)

# Split proportions (of all effects)
prop <- c(train = 0.7, valid = 0.15, test = 0.15)

# Partition data based on outcome
set_split <- split(df, df$replicate)

# Set sizes per stratum
n_train <- lapply(set_split, \(set) round(nrow(set) * prop[["train"]]))
n_valid <- lapply(set_split, \(set) round(nrow(set) * prop[["valid"]]))

# Training sample per stratum
train_smpl <- mapply(\(set, n) sample(set$eid, n), set_split, n_train)
train_eid <- unlist(train_smpl)
train_ind <- df$eid %in% train_eid

# Validation sample per stratum, from the rest
valid_smpl <- mapply(
  \(set, n) sample(setdiff(set$eid, train_eid), n),
  set_split,
  n_valid
)
valid_ind <- df$eid %in% unlist(valid_smpl)

# Combined sets
strat_diy <- list(
  train = df[train_ind, ],
  valid = df[valid_ind, ],
  test = df[!train_ind & !valid_ind, ]
)
```

::: {.callout-important title="Changed since submission"}
- One pass from the whole data: both set sizes per stratum count from all effects, and the validation sample is drawn from what the training sample left.
- Returns the list `strat_diy` (train, valid, test) instead of separate sets.
- Lambdas and `set$eid`, as in Listing 7.
:::

#### Listing 9

Code to do a 70/30 simple random split and a 70/15/15 stratified split with the `partition()` function of the adatutor package.

```{r listing-9}
# Simple random split (two way)
set.seed(112)
rand_split <- partition(df, prop = 0.7)

# Stratified split (three way)
set.seed(112)
strat_split <- partition(df, prop = c(0.7, 0.15, 0.15), strata = "replicate")

# Verification
mapply(identical, strat_diy, strat_split)
```

::: {.callout-note title="Add to tutorial"}
For applied work, we recommend `partition()` or the `rsample` package (Listing 10) over the code of Listings 4 to 8. `partition()` checks its inputs and avoids a pitfall of `sample()`: `sample(x, k)` reads a single number `x` as `1:x`. Listings 4 and 5 sample row positions, so with one row left they would draw a row that does not exist. (Listings 7 and 8 sample the character ids in `eid`, which are safe.) `partition()` draws positions with `sample.int()`, which has no such special case.
:::

::: {.callout-important title="Changed since submission"}
- `partition()` replaces `random_split()` and `stratified_split()`.
- The stratified split is now 70/15/15, with a check against Listing 8.
:::

#### Listing 10

Code to do a 70/30 simple random split and a 70/15/15 stratified split with the `rsample` package.

```{r listing-10}
# Install once: install.packages("rsample")

# Simple random split (two way)
set.seed(112)
rand_split_pkg <- rsample::initial_split(df, prop = 0.7)
train_pkg <- rsample::training(rand_split_pkg)
test_pkg <- rsample::testing(rand_split_pkg)

# Stratified split (three way)
set.seed(112)
strat_split_pkg <- rsample::initial_validation_split(
  df,
  prop = c(0.7, 0.15),
  strata = "replicate"
)

# Training, validation, and test sets
train_pkg <- rsample::training(strat_split_pkg)
valid_pkg <- rsample::validation(strat_split_pkg)
test_pkg <- rsample::testing(strat_split_pkg)
```

::: {.callout-note title="Add to tutorial"}
The adatutor package is built for teaching: its functions show the mechanics and stay small, even though `partition()` is fast. For applied work, a full machine-learning infrastructure such as tidymodels [@tidymodels] is the better home. It offers cross-validation, bootstraps, and nested resampling through `rsample` [@rsample], many more models through `parsnip`, and tuning workflows around them. The move is short, because adatutor follows the same conventions: `initial_split()` takes the same `prop` and `strata` arguments as `partition()`, models are fitted with a formula and a data frame, and predictions come from `predict()` with a `type` argument.
:::

::: {.callout-important title="Changed since submission"}
- `rsample::` calls instead of `library(rsample)`, with an install line.
- The stratified split is now 70/15/15, with `initial_validation_split()`, as in Listing 9; each split re-seeded.
- Object names `rand_split_pkg`, `strat_split_pkg`, `train_pkg`, `valid_pkg`, `test_pkg` instead of `randsplit`, `stratsplit`, `train`, `testvalid`.
:::

#### Figure 1 

Leave-one-group-out cross-validation (LOGO-CV), with the replication projects as the groups. From left to right, the data are first divided into six projects: Many Labs 1 (ML1, 13 study effects), the Replication Project Psychology (RPP, 90), Many Labs 3 (ML3, 10), the Experimental Economics Replication Project (EERP, 18), the Social Science Replication Project (SSRP, 21), and Many Labs 2 (ML2, 24), 176 study effects in all. A seventh project, the decision-market replications of Holzmeister et al. (HOLZ, 26), is held back for the final test and takes no part in the cross-validation. Row heights are proportional to project size, but no row is shorter than 6% of the total height, so ML3 appears slightly larger than its share. In Iteration 1, ML1 is the test set, and the model is trained on the other five projects. After training, the model is evaluated on the held-out ML1 study effects. The same steps are repeated with each of the other projects as the test set (Iterations 2--6), which yields six performance estimates. It is tempting to summarize them in a single number, but taken together, they give a richer picture of how well the model carries over to a new project.

```{r figure-1}
tutplot_logoscheme(
  df$pid,
  levels = c("ml1", "rpp", "ml3", "eerp", "ssrp", "ml2")
)
```

::: {.callout-important title="Changed since submission"}
- New figure.
:::

#### Listing [NEW]

Code to restore the stratified split from the package.

```{r restore-split}
# Load the split
data(altmext_splits)

# The split used before LOGO-CV takes over
train <- altmext_splits$train
valid <- altmext_splits$valid
test <- altmext_splits$test
```

::: {.callout-note title="Add to tutorial"}
Module 1 showed several ways to split the data. Modules 2 to 5 and the first listings of Module 6 build on the stratified 70/15/15 split of Listing 8: they fit on the training set and predict the test set. The package ships this split as `altmext_splits`, so it loads in one line instead of rerunning Module 1. With only 202 study effects, however, a test set of 31 gives a rough estimate at best, and a validation set of 30 leaves little room for tuning. From Listing 32 on, we therefore switch to LOGO-CV (Figure 1), in which every project serves as the test set in turn; the validation set stays unused.

# Module 2: Classification Stumps

#### Listing 11

Code to tabulate the outcome on both sides of the power cut.

```{r listing-11}
# Condition for the split
split_cond <- train$power.o < 0.927

# Study effects with power.o < 0.927
table(train$replicate[split_cond])

# Study effects with power.o >= 0.927
table(train$replicate[!split_cond])
```

::: {.callout-important title="Changed since submission"}
- The cut is 0.927 on `altmext` (0.9305 on `altmejd`); `split_cond` instead of `splitcond`.
:::

#### Listing 12

Code to set the hyperparameters of a classification tree and fit the model to
the training data.

```{r listing-12}
# Fit classification stump
cstump <- rpart::rpart(
  replicate ~ power.o + n.o,
  data = train[, voi_nms],
  # Classification tree
  method = "class",
  # Maximum depth
  maxdepth = 1,
  # Gini impurity (default)
  parms = list(split = "gini"),
  # Keep the training data (Figures 2 and 3)
  model = TRUE
)
```

::: {.callout-important title="Changed since submission"}
- Two predictors (`power.o + n.o`), the ones Figure 2 shows, instead of all four (`replicate ~ .`). Module 3 switches to all four in Listing 19.
- `maxdepth` and `parms` passed directly instead of `treehypar <- rpart.control(...)`. The submitted `rpart.control(split = "gini")` was wrong: `split` belongs in `parms`.
- `rpart::rpart()` instead of `library(rpart)`; `model = TRUE` keeps the training data for the figures.
:::

#### Figure 2

A classification tree of depth one or, equivalently, a classification stump. The stump was fitted to the training data using two reviewer metrics: the power and the sample size of the original study. The upper rectangle is the root node, the two lower rectangles are the leaf nodes. The root node is split at a power of 0.927. The left leaf node contains about 63% of the training data and the right leaf node about 37%. The label in each node ("success", "failure") is the stump's prediction for each study effect in that node. For example, the left leaf predicts failure for every study effect with a power below 0.927. In the training data, 62 of these 89 study effects did fail.

```{r figure-2}
# The stump of Listing 12, as a tree
tutplot_cstump(cstump, extra = 102)
```

::: {.callout-important title="Changed since submission"}
- Drawn by `tutplot_cstump()` from the stump of Listing 12 (`cstump_int` is gone).
- On `altmext`: 0.927, 63% / 37%, 62 of 89 (submitted: 0.9305, 62% / 38%, 49 of 66).
:::

Listing 12 now fits the stump behind Figure 2, so this listing reproduces the figure exactly. The four-predictor stump (`p_value.o` at 0.0007, leaves 90 and 51) first appears in Listing 19.

#### Figure 3

The decision boundary of a classification stump. The x-axis shows the power of the original study, the y-axis its sample size. So the y-axis does not show the outcome variable, but a second study characteristic. Because a classification stump is a tree of depth one, only one characteristic, power, separates successfully replicated study effects from failed ones. The decision boundary is the vertical line at a power of 0.927. The stump predicts success for every point in the green region and failure for every point in the blue region. Yellow dots are study effects that replicated, according to the replication metric; purple dots are those that failed. Thus, yellow dots in the blue region are misclassifications, and so are purple dots in the green region.

```{r figure-3}
# The stump of Listing 12, as the boundary it draws
tutplot_boundary(
  cstump,
  data = train,
  xlab = "Power (Original Study)",
  ylab = "Sample Size (Original Study)"
)
```

::: {.callout-important title="Changed since submission"}
- New chunk: the submitted figure had no code. Drawn by `tutplot_boundary()` from the stump of Listing 12.
- Axis labels (R1.C7) and viridis colors: blue and green regions, purple and yellow dots, a color-bar legend. The caption follows (submitted: gray triangles and blue circles).
:::

#### Figure 4

The Gini impurity for a two-class classification problem. The x-axis is the proportion of Class 1 (e.g., the proportion of successes in the empirical example). The y-axis is the Gini impurity. The Gini impurity is highest when both classes are equally frequent, that is, when the proportion of Class 1 is 0.5 and there are as many successes as failures. The more homogeneous a node becomes, the lower its impurity. It is zero when a node holds only one class (only successes or only failures).

```{r figure-4}
# Visualize
tutplot_gini(x_seq = seq(0.01, 1, by = 0.01), lwd = 2)
```

::: {.callout-important title="Changed since submission"}
- Drawn by `tutplot_gini()`: one viridis color and a grid, as in Figures 6 and 7.
:::

#### Listing 14

Code to calculate the midpoints between adjacent power values and find the
position of the split value.

```{r listing-14}
# Sorted vector
power_srt <- sort(train$power.o)

# Adjacent means
adjmeans <- (power_srt[-1] + power_srt[-length(power_srt)]) / 2

# Find position of value '0.927'
which(round(adjmeans, 4) == 0.927)
```

::: {.callout-important title="Changed since submission"}
- Because of the new data, the cut is 0.927, at position 89 (submitted: 0.9305).
:::

```{r gini-byhand}
# Gini impurity of the two leaves and of the split, from the counts in Figure 2
gini <- function(p) 1 - (p^2 + (1 - p)^2)
gini_left <- gini(27 / 89)
gini_right <- gini(40 / 52)
(89 * gini_left + 52 * gini_right) / 141
```

::: {.callout-note title="Check in tutorial"}
The equation block after Listing 14 regenerates: failure leaf 62 of 89 and 27 of 89, Gini 0.423; success leaf 12 of 52 and 40 of 52, Gini 0.355; split 89/141 · 0.423 + 52/141 · 0.355 ≈ 0.398 (submitted: 49/66, 17/66 → 0.382; 10/41, 31/41 → 0.369; 66/107, 41/107 → 0.377).
:::

#### Listing 15

Code to make the assumption of equal weights explicit.

```{r listing-15}
# Number of rows
m <- nrow(train)

# Equal weight to each observation
D <- rep(1, m) / m

# Fit classification stump
cstump_eq <- rpart::rpart(
  replicate ~ power.o + n.o,
  data = train[, voi_nms],
  method = "class",
  maxdepth = 1,
  # Equal weights
  weights = D
)

# Visualize
sty <- viridis_tree(cstump_eq)
cstump_eq |>
  rpart.plot::rpart.plot(
    extra = 100,
    digits = 4,
    box.col = sty$box,
    col = sty$text
  )
```

::: {.callout-important title="Changed since submission"}
- Two predictors, as in Listing 12; `cstump_eq` instead of overwriting `cstump`.
- `weights = D`: the submitted `weight = D` relied on partial argument matching.
- `rpart::rpart()`, `rpart.plot::rpart.plot()` and `viridis_tree()` instead of `library()` calls and `box.palette = "BuGy"`.
:::

#### Listing 16

Code to show the sensitivity to observation weights by using normalized random
weights from a uniform distribution.

```{r listing-16}
# For reproducibility
set.seed(112)

# Draws from standard uniform
D_raw <- runif(m)

# Normalize (sum to 1)
D <- D_raw / sum(D_raw)

# Fit classification stump
cstump_ast <- rpart::rpart(
  replicate ~ power.o + n.o,
  data = train[, voi_nms],
  method = "class",
  maxdepth = 1,
  # Random weights
  weights = D
)

# Visualize
sty <- viridis_tree(cstump_ast)
cstump_ast |>
  rpart.plot::rpart.plot(
    extra = 100,
    digits = 4,
    box.col = sty$box,
    col = sty$text
  )
```

::: {.callout-note title="Add to tutorial"}
With the random weights, the stump still splits on power, but at a different value: 0.921 instead of 0.927 (Figure 5). Each weighting scheme changes which split has the lowest weighted Gini impurity, so the decision rule moves with the weights. With more predictors, the split variable itself can change: on all four reviewer metrics, random weights make the stump split on the *p* value in about three of four random weightings and on power in the rest.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Check in tutorial"}
The paragraph before `lst:sensitive` says that with random weights "a different study characteristic now yields the lowest overall Gini impurity ... one of the p-values". That compared the two-predictor Figure 2 with a four-predictor stump. Replace it with the box above. Checked over seeds 1 to 1,000 with normalized `runif()` weights: with `power.o + n.o`, the stump always splits on power (cut 0.55 to 0.93); with all four predictors, it splits 716 times on the *p* value and 284 times on power.
:::

::: {.callout-important title="Changed since submission"}
- `runif(m)` instead of `runif(107)`: the literal breaks whenever `train` has another size, the likely cause of the error in R2.C5. Module 1 now ends by restoring `altmext_splits`, so `train` is the same for every reader.
- Two predictors, as in Listing 12; `weights = D` (submitted: `weight = D`).
:::

# Module 3: AdaBoost

#### Listing 17

Code to understand the givens in the AdaBoost algorithm.

```{r listing-17}
# Predictors and outcome (names)
pred_nms
out_nme

# Predictor matrix
x_train <- train[, pred_nms]

# Outcome vector
y_train <- train[, out_nme]

# Indices
i <- 1
m <- nrow(train)

# i-th row or element
x_train[i, ]
y_train[i]

# i-th to m-th row (i.e., all)
cbind(x_train, y_train)[i:m, ]
```

::: {.callout-note title="Check in tutorial"}
The prose cites line numbers for Listings 17 (Line 2; Lines 4 and 6), 20 (Lines 2 and 4) and 23 (Line 4; Lines 6 to 8). Renumber them after porting: the script's listings have blank lines, and Listing 17 now has one statement per line.
:::

::: {.callout-important title="Changed since submission"}
- `pred_nms` and `out_nme` (`prednms`, `outnme`); one statement per line instead of `;`.
:::

#### Listing 18

Code to generate initialization weights in the AdaBoost algorithm.

```{r listing-18}
# Initialization weights
D1 <- rep(1, m) / m
```

#### Listing 19

Code to fit a classification stump with the initialization weights.

```{r listing-19}
# Fit classification stump with the initialization weights
h1 <- rpart::rpart(
  replicate ~ .,
  data = train[, voi_nms],
  method = "class",
  maxdepth = 1,
  parms = list(split = "gini"),
  weights = D1
)
```

::: {.callout-important title="Changed since submission"}
- `maxdepth` and `parms` passed directly instead of `treehypar <- rpart.control(maxdepth = 1, split = "gini")`, which was wrong: `split` belongs in `parms`.
- `rpart::rpart()` instead of `rpart()`. All four predictors, as submitted: this is the stump of the Listing 13 note (`p_value.o` at 0.0007, leaves 90 and 51).
:::

#### Listing 20

Code to calculate the classification stump's error.

```{r listing-20}
# Retrodictions (training data)
y_retro <- predict(h1, newdata = train[, pred_nms], type = "class")

# Retrodictive error
epsilon <- sum(D1 * (y_retro != y_train))
```

::: {.callout-important title="Changed since submission"}
- `y_retro` (`yretro`); `newdata = train[, pred_nms]` (`voinms`), as in Listing 24 and Module 5.
:::

#### Listing 21

Code to calculate the classification stump's performance.

```{r listing-21}
# Retrodictive performance
perf <- sum(D1 * (y_retro == y_train))

# Retrodictive error
epsilon <- 1 - perf
```

#### Listing 22

Code to calculate the classification stump's weight assuming a learning rate eta of 1.

```{r listing-22}
# Learning rate
eta <- 1

# Model weight
alpha1 <- 0.5 * log(perf / epsilon) * eta
```

::: {.callout-important title="Changed since submission"}
- `0.5` instead of `1/2`, as in Listing 24 and in the package.
:::

#### Figure 6

The model weight of a classification stump ($\alpha_t$) as a function of its performance ($1-\epsilon_t$), for three learning rates ($\eta$). The better a stump performs, the larger its weight; equivalently, the lower its error ($\epsilon_t$), the larger its weight. The learning rate scales the weight: $\eta = 1$ leaves it as it is, smaller values shrink it. The dot marks the first stump of Listing 22, with a performance of 0.730 and a model weight of 0.499. Module 7 shows how to choose the learning rate.

<!-- check the module numbers after the module split -->

```{r figure-6}
# Model weight by performance, for three learning rates; the dot is h1
tutplot_modelweight(eta = c(1, 0.5, 0.1), marked_perf = perf)
```

::: {.callout-important title="Changed since submission"}
- Drawn by `tutplot_modelweight()`; the dot marks the first stump (performance 0.730, model weight 0.499).
- "Model weight" replaces "importance" on the y-axis and in the caption: Module 4 uses "importance" for predictors.
:::

#### Listing 23

Code to calculate the update factor for the initialization weights.

```{r listing-23}
# Indicator trick
chi1 <- (y_retro == y_train) * 1 + (y_retro != y_train) * -1

# Unnormalized weights
D2_raw <- D1 * exp(-alpha1 * chi1)

# Normalization constant
Z1 <- sum(D2_raw)

# Normalized weights
D2 <- D2_raw / Z1
```

::: {.callout-important title="Changed since submission"}
- `y_retro` (`yretro`).
:::

#### Figure 7

The update factor ($e^{-\alpha_t\chi_t}$) by classification result, for three model weights. A correctly classified study effect has $\chi_t = 1$, and its weight shrinks for the next round by a factor below 1 (right). A misclassified one has $\chi_t = -1$, and its weight grows by a factor above 1 (left). The heavier the model, the stronger the update in both directions. The middle curve uses the first stump's model weight of 0.499; the other two use 0.7 and 0.3.

```{r figure-7}
# Three model weights: a heavier one, the first stump's, a lighter one
alpha_int <- c(0.7, round(alpha1, 3), 0.3)

# Visualize
tutplot_updatefactor(alpha = alpha_int)
```

:::

The weights of the first 25 study effects in the training set before ($D_1$, purple) and after ($D_2$, teal) the first round. Every initial weight is 1/141. #### Listing 24

Code to loop through the algorithmic steps. It takes a few seconds.

```{r listing-24}
# Number of trees, T
n_tree <- 1000

# Learning rate
eta <- 1

# List of models and weights
ada_diy <- vector("list", n_tree)

# Initial observation weights
D <- rep(1, m) / m

# Loop through steps
for (t in seq_len(n_tree)) {
  h <- rpart::rpart(
    replicate ~ .,
    data = train[, voi_nms],
    method = "class",
    maxdepth = 1,
    weights = D
  )
  y_retro <- predict(h, newdata = train[, pred_nms], type = "class")
  epsilon <- sum(D * (y_retro != y_train))
  alpha <- 0.5 * log((1 - epsilon) / epsilon) * eta
  chi <- (y_retro == y_train) * 1 + (y_retro != y_train) * -1
  D_raw <- D * exp(-alpha * chi)
  D <- D_raw / sum(D_raw)
  ada_diy[[t]] <- list(h = h, alpha = alpha)
}
names(ada_diy) <- paste0("t", seq_len(n_tree))

# First model weight, as a check against Listing 22
cat("Model weight 1:", ada_diy$t1$alpha)
```

::: {.callout-note title="Check in tutorial"}

Also: the Listing 24 caption says "about a minute", now a few seconds; `fit` → `ada_diy` in the Loop and Result prose; "Retrodivitve" in Listing 21; $a_t$ → $\alpha_t$ in Eq. ensemble, Eq. ensemble2, the algorithm box (Step 3 and Result) and Exercise 3.2's update factor; "Module 4" (five mentions) → the hyperparameter module after the split. After the split, the algorithm box of the Epilogue closes Module 3; the ensemble equation ("Result") and the boundary figure move to Module 5.
:::

#### The Package Solution [NEW]

Code to fit the same ensemble with the adatutor package.

```{r listing-24-pkg}
# The same stump, fitted without weights: adaboost() sets its own
cstump_fit <- rpart::rpart(
  replicate ~ .,
  data = train[, voi_nms],
  method = "class",
  maxdepth = 1,
  parms = list(split = "gini"),
  # Keep the training data: adaboost() refits the stump from it
  model = TRUE
)

# Boost it
ada_fit <- cstump_fit |> adaboost(n_iter = n_tree, eta = eta)

# Verification: the model weights agree, round by round
identical(sapply(ada_diy, "[[", "alpha"), sapply(ada_fit, "[[", "alpha"))
```

::: {.callout-note title="Add to tutorial"}
Both fits carry the same model weights, round by round. From here on, we therefore use `adaboost()`. It saves typing, and it adds checks and messages that support readers as they explore the algorithm: it shows its progress and refuses a tree it cannot refit as handed in, for example one fitted with `weights`. Readers who prefer their own code can continue with Listing 24.

`adaboost()` takes the fitted stump as its first argument. This makes explicit what is often taken for granted: the weak learner is a classification stump. The algorithm itself accepts any weak learner that performs better than chance (Equation `Eq:perfgreat`). The weak learner is thus a hyperparameter in its own right, and other models can be boosted as well, from deeper trees to single-layer perceptrons. Because the learner is a fitted tree, its settings travel with it: `adaboost()` carries the tree's `maxdepth`, `cp` and the other `rpart.control()` values into every round, which is why it has no `maxdepth` argument of its own. It accepts only classification trees, the models Module 2 introduced. Stumps are a convenient choice: their simplicity keeps the ensemble interpretable, as Module 4 shows.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Add to tutorial"}
Repeat the handoff sentence after each later `identical()` check, with its listing: "The two match, so we continue with the package function: it keeps the listings short and saves typing. Readers who prefer their own code can continue with Listing N." The places: Module 4 (`gauge()`, the importance loop), Module 5 (retrodictions, Listing 25; the margin; predictions, Listing 28), Module 6 (`logo_cv()`, the LOGO-CV loop) and Module 7 (`hypergrid`, the grid loop). Not after `auroc()` or `assess()`, which have no by-hand counterpart. A reader who stays fully by hand pastes Listing 24 into the loops of Modules 6 and 7.
:::

# Module 4: A Glimpse at Feature Importance

::: {.callout-note title="Check in tutorial"}
The whole module is new (R1.C6). The "Add to tutorial" boxes hold the prose, the listing intros and the caption stay plain, and the two boxes marked "(box)" are manuscript boxes. Number the three listings and the figure when porting; the boundary figure of Module 5 becomes Figure 10. Decide then whether the walk-through cites line numbers. Numbers: 33.7, 23.6, 21.6 and 21.1 percent; 97 of 1,000 stumps; in the deep box 32.2, 26.0, 24.2 and 17.6 percent.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Add to tutorial"}
In the Introduction, we set out to turn AdaBoost into a "glass box" tool for applied work. So far, this meant taking the algorithm apart, inspecting its nuts and bolts, and rebuilding it in code. Now we put this knowledge to work and inspect the fitted ensemble, asking which predictors does the model rely on as it learns? This is the question of feature importance, part of the wider field of interpretable machine learning. Because this tutorial is about AdaBoost, we only scratch the surface and develop one model-specific measure for boosted stumps. Model-agnostic methods, such as permutation importance and effect plots, go much further. Readers who want to learn more can start with @molnar2025 or @pargent2023.
**TODO** tidy models book julia sige?

Most importance measures for tree ensembles build on two quantities: how often a predictor is used to split (split frequency) and how much its splits reduce impurity (gain). For stumps, we build on the first and weight each split by the stump's model weight. The result is a *relative importance* score: each predictor's share, in percent, of the model weight of all stumps that split. Two facts from earlier modules make this work. In Module 2, we showed that a stump splits at most once, with one yes/no question about one predictor. In Module 3, we derived each stump's model weight $\alpha_t$, which grows with its performance on the weighted data. To get the importance score, we simply group the stumps by the predictor they split on and sum their model weights. Why does this make sense? AdaBoost shifts weight toward the study effects the ensemble still gets wrong, so each new stump works on the ensemble's largest mistakes. A predictor that many stumps choose, particularly stumps with large model weights, is one the ensemble relies on again and again for its corrections. Thus, the summed weight shows how much the ensemble relies on each predictor, relative to the others. Listing [NEW] puts this into code.
:::

#### Listing [NEW]

Code to compute the relative importance of each predictor from the boosted stumps.

```{r importance-diy}
# One entry per predictor, starting at zero
imp_diy <- setNames(numeric(length(pred_nms)), pred_nms)

# Loop through stumps
for (t in seq_along(ada_fit)) {
  h <- ada_fit[[t]]$h
  # The predictor at the root: the one the stump splits on
  pred_nme <- h$frame$var[1]
  # A stump that does not split has a leaf at the root: skip it
  if (pred_nme == "<leaf>") {
    next
  }
  # Add the stump's model weight to its predictor
  imp_diy[pred_nme] <- imp_diy[pred_nme] + ada_fit[[t]]$alpha
}

# Relative importance: each predictor's share, in percent
imp_diy <- imp_diy / sum(imp_diy) * 100

# Most important first
sort(imp_diy, decreasing = TRUE)
```

::: {.callout-note title="Add to tutorial"}
The listing starts with a named vector of zeros, one entry per predictor. The loop then adds each stump's model weight, `ada_fit[[t]]$alpha`, to the entry of the predictor the stump splits on. `rpart()` stores that predictor in `frame`, the tree's table of nodes. Its first row is the root, so for a stump, `frame$var[1]` is the predictor it splits on. A stump may also not split at all. Then `frame$var[1]` reads `<leaf>`, and `next` skips the stump; the box below explains why this happens. Finally, we divide by the total and multiply by 100, so the scores sum to 100 and read as percentages. With our training data, the p value of the original study takes about a third of the weight; power, sample size, and effect size share the rest almost evenly. The loop runs unchanged on the ensemble of Listing 24, because both fits store `h` and `alpha` per round.

Footnote, at `ada_fit[[t]]$alpha`: The listings use `$` because most readers know it. In functions of their own, readers are better served by `[[` with the full name, for example `[["alpha"]]` instead of `$alpha`. `$` completes partial names silently, so a typo such as `$alph` still returns the model weight instead of an error; `[["alph"]]` returns `NULL`, which is easy to spot. The listing in the box on deeper trees uses this form.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Add to tutorial (box)"}
**Why would a stump not split?** By default, `rpart()` keeps a split only if it decreases the overall lack of fit by at least a factor of the complexity parameter, `cp = 0.01`, and only if both leaves hold enough study effects (`minsplit`, `minbucket`). As the weights shift toward a few hard study effects, a split that passes may not exist. With our training data, 97 of the 1,000 stumps consist of a bare root. Such a stump has no predictor to credit, so the loop skips it.
:::

::: {.callout-important title="Changed since submission"}
- New listing (R1.C6). It loops over `ada_fit`, the fit the handoff after Listing 24 switched to.
:::

#### The Package Solution [NEW]

Code to compute the same importance with the adatutor package.

```{r importance-pkg}
# Relative importance from the package
imp_fit <- gauge(ada_fit)
plot(imp_fit)

# The package's shares as a named vector, like imp_diy
imp_vec <- setNames(imp_fit$importance, imp_fit$variable)

# Verification: the same shares, most important first
identical(sort(imp_diy, decreasing = TRUE), imp_vec)
```

::: {.callout-note title="Add to tutorial"}
`gauge()` computes the same measure for the whole ensemble and returns a data frame with one row per predictor, most important first. The two match, so we continue with the package function: it keeps the listings short and saves typing. Readers who prefer their own code can continue with the listing above. `gauge()` also handles deeper trees (see the box below), and its `plot()` method draws the result as a lollipop chart (Figure [NEW]).

The numbers are relative: they show how the ensemble divided its weight, not what a predictor is worth on its own. They carry no sign, so they do not say whether a high p value helps or hurts a replication. Correlated predictors share their weight, and the ranking changes with the hyperparameters and the training data.
:::

::: {.callout-important title="Changed since submission"}
- New listing (R1.C6): `gauge()` and its `plot()` method are new in the package.
:::

#### Figure [NEW]

The relative importance of the four predictors in the 1,000 boosted stumps of Module 3. For each predictor, the line and dot show the summed model weights of the stumps that split on it, as a percentage of the total. The p value of the original study carries about a third of the weight. Power, sample size, and effect size share the rest, with between 21 and 24 percent each.

```{r figure-importance}

tutplot_importance(imp_fit)
```

::: {.callout-important title="Changed since submission"}
- New figure (R1.C6), drawn by `tutplot_importance()` on the result of `gauge()`. The `plot()` call of the package listing draws the same chart.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Add to tutorial (box)"}
**Deeper trees: split frequency meets gain.** Deeper trees can split on several predictors. Then each tree's model weight is shared among the predictors it uses, in proportion to how much their splits reduce the Gini impurity of Module 2 (the gain). The measure becomes a mix: the model weight decides how much a tree counts, and the gain decides how its share is divided. This is a weighted version of the mean decrease in impurity. The loop changes in two places: it reads `variable.importance`, rpart's gain per predictor, instead of the root's predictor, and it adds a share per predictor instead of the whole weight.

```{r importance-deep}
# A depth-4 tree instead of a stump, boosted for ten rounds
ada_deep <- rpart::rpart(
  replicate ~ .,
  data = train[, voi_nms],
  method = "class",
  maxdepth = 4,
  model = TRUE
) |>
  adaboost(n_iter = 10, eta = 1)

imp_deep <- setNames(numeric(length(pred_nms)), pred_nms)
for (t in seq_along(ada_deep)) {
  h <- ada_deep[[t]][["h"]]
  # rpart's gain per predictor; NULL if the tree did not split
  gain <- h[["variable.importance"]]
  if (is.null(gain)) {
    next
  }
  # Split the tree's model weight across its predictors, by their gain
  share <- ada_deep[[t]][["alpha"]] * (gain / sum(gain))
  imp_deep[names(share)] <- imp_deep[names(share)] + share
}
imp_deep <- imp_deep / sum(imp_deep) * 100
sort(imp_deep, decreasing = TRUE)
```

For a stump, `gain` holds one number, so `gain / sum(gain)` is 1 and the whole model weight goes to its one predictor. The gain still decides which predictor a stump picks, but not how much weight it gets. `gauge()` runs this general version, which is why it matched the stump loop exactly. Unlike `variable.importance`, it credits primary splits only, so the surrogate splits that `rpart()` fits by default do not change its result. It also runs on data with missing predictor values: `adaboost()` sends a study effect whose split variable is missing with the majority of its node, and `rpart()` scores a split on the cases where the predictor is observed.
:::

#### Listing 25

Code to generate ensemble retrodictions.

```{r listing-25}
# Boosted classification stumps
h_fit <- lapply(ada_fit, "[[", "h")

# Model weights
alpha_fit <- sapply(ada_fit, "[[", "alpha")

# Retrodictions from stumps
y_retro_cstp <- sapply(
  h_fit,
  predict,
  newdata = train[, pred_nms],
  type = "vector"
)

# Recode the classes 1 and 2 to -1 and 1
y_retro_1m1 <- 2 * y_retro_cstp - 3

# Weighted vote across all stumps
retro_mgn_diy <- as.vector(alpha_fit %*% t(y_retro_1m1))

# Retrodictions from full model: the vote's sign
y_retro_diy <- sign(retro_mgn_diy)
```

::: {.callout-important title="Changed since submission"}
- `ada_fit`, `h_fit`, `alpha_fit` (was `fit`, `h`, `a`) and `pred_nms` (was `prednms`); `y_retro_cstp` and `y_retro_1m1` (was `yretro_stumps`, overwritten by the recode).
- The vote in its own object, `retro_mgn_diy`, as a plain vector (`as.vector()`; the submitted `a %*% t(...)` left a 1-by-m matrix), and `y_retro_diy` as its sign (was `yretro_ada`). The `sapply()` call is spread over lines.
:::

#### Listing 26

Code to replace matrix multiplication with a loop.

```{r listing-26}
# The same vote, one study effect at a time
y_retro_loop <- numeric(m)
for (i in seq_len(m)) {
  y_retro_loop[i] <- sign(sum(alpha_fit * y_retro_1m1[i, ]))
}

# Verification
identical(y_retro_loop, y_retro_diy)
```

::: {.callout-important title="Changed since submission"}
- The loop runs and verifies itself: `i` as the index (the submitted loop used `m` as both the count and the index), `alpha_fit` and `y_retro_1m1` (was `a`, `yretro_stumps`), and the result in `y_retro_loop` with an `identical()` check instead of overwriting the matrix product.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Add to tutorial"}
Equation `Eq:ensemble` takes the sign of a weighted sum. That sum has a name, the *margin*. The package's `predict()` returns either: `type = "class"` applies `sign()`, as Listing 25 does, and keeps only the direction of the vote; `type = "margin"` returns the sum itself, with its size, that is, how far the vote is from the tie at zero.
:::

#### The Package Solution [NEW]

Code to generate the same retrodictions with the adatutor package, as class labels and as margins.

```{r listing-25-pkg}
# Retrodictions from the full model: class labels, the vote's sign
y_retro_cls <- predict(ada_fit, newdata = train[, pred_nms], type = "class")

# The weighted vote itself, before sign(): the margin
y_retro_mgn <- predict(ada_fit, newdata = train[, pred_nms], type = "margin")

# Verification
identical(y_retro_diy, y_retro_cls)
identical(retro_mgn_diy, y_retro_mgn)
```

::: {.callout-note title="Add to tutorial"}
Both match, the class labels and the margins, so we continue with the package function: it keeps the listings short and saves typing. Readers who prefer their own code can continue with Listing 25. Note the message both calls printed. `predict()` noticed that the data it scored are the data the ensemble was trained on, and says so: the outputs are retrodictions, not predictions. Keep the margin in mind for Module 6: a class label can only be right or wrong, while the margin carries the ranking that measures like the area under the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve need.
:::

#### Figure 10

The decision boundary of 1,000 boosted classification stumps: the stump of Figure 3, boosted as in Listing 24. The x-axis shows the power of the original study, the y-axis its sample size. So the y-axis does not show the outcome variable, but a second study characteristic. The shading shows the margin, the weighted vote of Listing 25, on the color scale above the panel: purple where the ensemble votes for failure, yellow where it votes for success, and teal in between, where the vote is close to a tie. The further a color sits from that middle, the larger the vote. The black lines are the boundary, where the margin is zero. Yellow dots are study effects that replicated, according to the replication metric; purple dots are those that failed. Where the stump of Figure 3 draws one vertical line, the ensemble cuts the plane into many rectangles, because each stump splits on one of the two predictors.

```{r figure-10}
# The two-predictor stump of Figure 3, boosted as in Listing 24
ada_two <- cstump |> adaboost(n_iter = n_tree, eta = eta, verbose = FALSE)

# The same call as Figure 3, with the ensemble in place of the stump
tutplot_boundary(
  ada_two,
  data = train,
  xlab = "Power (Original Study)",
  ylab = "Sample Size (Original Study)"
)
```

## Performance Measures

::: {.callout-note title="Add to tutorial"}
After predicting the test set, we can evaluate the ensemble by comparing its predictions with the observed outcomes. The confusion matrix of Listing 29 is the starting point. A first measure is *accuracy*, the share of correct predictions: the sum of the main diagonal divided by the sum of all entries. Accuracy needs a baseline, however. The *base rate* of the test set, the share of its study effects that replicated, is 0.48, so a model that always predicts failure is right 52 percent of the time without having learned anything. Remember also that the dataset is imbalanced: more study effects failed than replicated, and accuracy hides which class the errors fall on. *Balanced accuracy* corrects for this. It is the mean of *sensitivity*, the share of successes the ensemble predicts as successes, and *specificity*, the share of failures it predicts as failures [see @pargent2023, who warn that the error rate alone says little under imbalance].

These measures read the class labels, so they judge one decision: the sign of the vote. The margin of Module 5 carries more, namely how far each study effect sits from the tie, and with it a ranking of the study effects. Two measures read that ranking. The *area under the receiver operating characteristic curve* (AUROC, often just AUC) is the chance that a randomly drawn success scores higher than a randomly drawn failure [@bradley1997]. A random ranking scores 0.5, a perfect one 1, and the base rate plays no part. The *area under the precision-recall curve* (AUPRC) asks how pure the top of the ranking is at every cutoff. Here the base rate does play a part: a random ranking scores about the base rate, not 0.5. A third view is a budget. When only a few replications can be run, what matters is the *precision among the top k*, the share of successes among the k study effects with the highest margins. Listing 31 computes each measure once. The last three need the margin. Class labels have only two values, so the ROC curve collapses to a single point, and the AUROC quietly becomes the balanced accuracy. Listing 31 shows it.
:::

#### Listing 31

Code showing different measures to evaluate the predictive performance of the ensemble.

```{r listing-31}
# Confusion matrix, as in Listing 29
conf_mat <- table(y_test, y_pred_cls)

# Accuracy: the share of correct predictions
sum(diag(conf_mat)) / sum(conf_mat)

# Base rate of the test set: the share of successes
mean(y_test == "success")

# Sensitivity: the share of successes predicted as success (1)
sens <- mean(y_pred_cls[y_test == "success"] == 1)

# Specificity: the share of failures predicted as failure (-1)
spec <- mean(y_pred_cls[y_test == "failure"] == -1)

# Balanced accuracy: their mean
(sens + spec) / 2

# AUROC on the class labels: the balanced accuracy again
auroc(y_test, y_pred_cls)

# Area under the ROC curve, scored on the margin
auroc(y_test, y_pred_mgn)

# Area under the precision-recall curve
auprc(y_test, y_pred_mgn)

# Precision among the five highest margins
patk(y_test, y_pred_mgn, k = 5)
```

::: {.callout-note title="Add to tutorial"}
With 1,000 stumps and a learning rate of 1, the ensemble predicts 19 of the 31 test study effects correctly, an accuracy of 0.61 against a majority rate of 0.52. Its balanced accuracy is 0.61, which the AUROC on the class labels repeats. Scored on the margin, its AUROC is 0.70 and its AUPRC 0.69, against a base rate of 0.48, and its precision among the top five is 0.8. A test set of 31 study effects makes every one of these numbers rough, which is the second reason, after the nested data, to move on to cross-validation.
:::

## Leave-One-Group-Out Cross-Validation

::: {.callout-note title="Add to tutorial"}
Module 1 motivated cross-validation by project. The question we want answered is how the ensemble fares on a replication project it has never seen, not on a random study effect from a project it was trained on. A random split answers the second question and lets every project into the training data. Holding out whole projects instead is a form of *leave-one-group-out cross-validation* (LOGO-CV, Figure 1), with the replication projects as the groups. @pargent2023 call this blocked resampling, and @roberts2017 show the same idea for spatial, temporal and hierarchical groups. Each project serves as the test set once while the ensemble is trained on the others, which yields one performance estimate per project. A fold must hold enough study effects of both classes. A project does; a single study effect does not.

Before cross-validating, we set aside the newest project, the decision-market replications of @holzmeister2024 (HOLZ, 26 study effects). It takes no part in the cross-validation or in the tuning of Module 7 and serves as the final test set in Module 8. The six remaining projects, 176 study effects, are the tuning data.

**Note**: this is the latest project so its a common procedure in time series predictions.

The result is a distribution of six estimates, one per project. It is tempting to average them, but we do not, for two reasons. The six folds share most of their training data and differ in size, from 10 to 90 study effects, so the usual standard error of the mean would be far too small [@bengio2004]. And the spread is the finding: it shows for which projects the reviewer metrics carry a signal and for which they do not.

Listing 32 runs LOGO-CV by hand. The first lines set HOLZ aside. `split()` then partitions the tuning data by `pid` into a list with one data frame per project, and `proj_nms` holds the project names. The loop takes each project as the test set and the other five as the training set, fits the ensemble of Listing 24 with the package functions of Modules 3 and 5, and stores the held-out margins together with the observed outcomes. Keeping the margins, rather than a summary, pays off twice: after the loop, two `sapply()` calls compute the AUROC and the base rate per project, and the next section resamples the same margins. `system.time()` tracks the run time, because the cost of a setting matters once models grow.
:::

#### Listing 32

Code to do a leave-one-group-out cross-validation.

```{r listing-32}
# Hold out the newest project for the final test (Module 8)
df_holz <- df[df$pid == "holz", ]
df_noholz <- df[df$pid != "holz", ]

# One data frame per tuning project
df_split <- split(df_noholz, df_noholz$pid)
proj_nms <- names(df_split)

# The held-out margins, one data frame per project
scores <- list()

runtime <- system.time({
  # LOGO-CV: each project is the test set once
  for (rp in proj_nms) {
    # Training and test set
    test_cv <- df_split[[rp]]
    train_cv <- df_noholz[df_noholz$pid != rp, ]
    # The ensemble of Listing 24, fitted to the training set
    cstump_cv <- rpart::rpart(
      replicate ~ .,
      data = train_cv[, voi_nms],
      method = "class",
      maxdepth = 1,
      parms = list(split = "gini"),
      model = TRUE
    )
    ada_cv <- cstump_cv |> adaboost(n_iter = n_tree, eta = eta, verbose = FALSE)
    # Margins for the held-out project, with the observed outcomes
    scores[[rp]] <- data.frame(
      actual = test_cv[, out_nme],
      score = predict(
        ada_cv,
        newdata = test_cv[, pred_nms],
        type = "margin",
        verbose = FALSE
      )
    )
  }
})

# Run time in seconds
runtime["elapsed"]

# AUROC per project
auc_cv <- sapply(scores, \(s) auroc(s$actual, s$score))
auc_cv

# Base rate per project
sapply(scores, \(s) mean(s$actual == "success"))
```

::: {.callout-note title="Add to tutorial"}
**A Third Look at Performance.** The AUROC runs from 0.48 in ML3 (base rate 0.30) to 0.91 in ML1 (base rate 0.85). In ML3, with 10 study effects, the ensemble ranks no better than chance. In EERP and ML1 it ranks well, and RPP, the largest project, sits at 0.63. So some projects are indeed harder to predict from the reviewer metrics than others, and the base rates differ as much as the estimates do: in ML1, 85 percent of the study effects replicated, in ML3 only 30 percent. This matters for every measure that cuts the margin at zero, because the ensemble cuts at the threshold it learned on training data with a base rate near 0.47, far from ML1's 0.85 or ML3's 0.30. Before we ask whether other hyperparameters do better (Module 7), we ask how firm each estimate is.
:::

The loop stores the held-out margins with the outcomes; the AUROC and the base rate per project are computed after it. `n_tree` and `eta` from Listing 24 instead of literal values; `verbose = FALSE` and no `message()` per project. ## Bootstrap Intervals per Project

::: {.callout-note title="Add to tutorial"}
Each estimate rests on one project, and the small projects hold few study effects: 10 in ML3, 13 in ML1. How much could an estimate move if the project had drawn different study effects? A *bootstrap* answers this. We resample the held-out study effects of a project with replacement, score the resample with the margins the ensemble already produced, and repeat this 1,000 times. The 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of the resampled AUROCs give a 95 percent interval. The ensemble stays fixed, so the interval shows the uncertainty that comes from the project's study effects, not from refitting. A resample that happens to hold one class only has no AUROC and is dropped; the number of dropped draws is worth reporting, because a large share means the interval is too narrow. Listing [NEW] does this for one project, and the package for all six.

The intervals are wide. RPP's 90 study effects give the narrowest, from 0.51 to 0.75; ML3's 10 give the widest, the whole range from 0 to 1, so its estimate of 0.48 says almost nothing. ML1's interval looks narrower than its 13 study effects warrant, because 12 percent of its draws held successes only and were dropped; the package warns about this. The widths follow the fold sizes, then, and so does the trust each estimate deserves. Note what the intervals do not give: an interval around the mean across projects. The folds share their training data and differ in size, so no simple formula yields an honest standard error for that mean [@bengio2004], which is one more reason to report the projects one by one.
:::

#### Listing [NEW]

Code to bootstrap the AUROC of one held-out project.

```{r listing-boot}
# Resample the held-out EERP study effects, rescore the fixed margins
set.seed(112)
eerp <- scores$eerp
auc_boot <- replicate(1000, {
  rows <- sample(nrow(eerp), replace = TRUE)
  auroc(eerp$actual[rows], eerp$score[rows])
})

# Draws with one class only have no AUROC: count them, then drop them
sum(is.na(auc_boot))
quantile(auc_boot, c(0.025, 0.975), na.rm = TRUE)
```

::: {.callout-important title="Changed since submission"}
- New listing (R1.C4.b).
:::

#### The Package Solution [NEW]

Code to bootstrap every held-out project with the adatutor package.

```{r listing-boot-pkg}
# Bootstrap every held-out project; the intervals attach to the result
set.seed(112)
logo_boot <- bootstrap(logo_ada, n_resample = 1000)

# AUROC per project with its 95 percent interval and the number of
# dropped draws
do.call(rbind, lapply(logo_boot$ci, \(ci) ci[ci$metric == "auroc", ]))
```

`bootstrap()` resamples each held-out project in turn and keeps the intervals with the result, for every measure of `assess()`. The EERP row matches Listing [NEW], because both start from the same seed and EERP is resampled first. Figure [NEW] draws the six estimates with their bands.

::: {.callout-note title="Add to tutorial (box, decide at port)"}
**Why a project, not a study effect?** Could the folds be finer, with each study effect held out in turn? Within a project, that fails. Take EERP, 18 study effects, 11 of them successes. Hold out one, train on the other 17, score the held-out one, and repeat for all 18. The AUROC over these 18 scores is exactly 0: every success ranks below every failure. The reviewer metrics are weak predictors, so the ensemble mostly learns the class balance of its training data. Hold out a success, and the training data hold one success fewer, so the model leans toward failure and gives the held-out success a low margin. Hold out a failure, and the opposite happens. The margin encodes which class was removed, and the ranking comes out backwards. An intercept-only model does the same, so the fold design is at fault, not AdaBoost. Within ML1 and ML3 the AUROC is 0 as well; in RPP, with 90 study effects, within-project leave-one-out (0.64) and the held-out-project estimate (0.62) agree. A fold must hold enough study effects of both classes, and a project does.

| project | n | within-project leave-one-out | held-out project |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|
| EERP | 18 | 0.000 | 0.714 |
| ML1 | 13 | 0.000 | 0.818 |
| ML3 | 10 | 0.000 | 0.619 |
| RPP | 90 | 0.635 | 0.620 |
| SSRP | 21 | 0.417 | 0.676 |

Measured at 10 stumps and a learning rate of 1 on the five submitted projects (findings §2); recompute at the tutorial's setting if the box stays.
:::

AR.R1.C1 says so, because the reviewer quotes the submitted winner.

- Exercise 4.2 is dropped: the random search is in the main text, and its runtime question is in the Random Search box. Exercise 3.3 goes with Module 6 or 7 at the exercises pass.
- The Module 3 handoff box lists "Module 7 (`hypergrid`, the grid loop)" as a handoff place and says the by-hand reader pastes Listing 24 into the loops of Modules 6 and 7. With `logo_cv()` inside Listing 34, the Module 7 handoff sits after the one-call package solution, and the by-hand reader pastes the loop of Listing 32 into Listing 34.
- The letter names the code changes latexdiff cannot show: the inner loop of Listing 34 replaced by `logo_cv()`, the grid column `n_iter` (was `T`), the stability columns, the two new package listings and the `hypergrid` listings.
- `hypergrid` is package data, covered by the install line of Module 1; `?hypergrid` names the build script (about an hour on four cores).

- Run time of Listing 34: about 2.5 minutes on this machine (submitted: about 3 minutes).
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Add to tutorial"}
Module 3 fixed the ensemble's hyperparameters by hand: stumps, 1,000 rounds, a learning rate of 1. Module 6 showed what that choice is worth on each project. This module searches for a better one. There are several strategies for hyperparameter optimization (HPO). The simplest is a *grid search*, which tries every combination of a few values per hyperparameter. A *random search* tries a random subset of those combinations. Model-based strategies, such as Bayesian optimization, choose the next setting from the results so far [see @bischl2023, for an overview]. We start with the grid and show the random search after it.

A boosted ensemble has hyperparameters at two levels. The weak learner has its own. Here that is the depth of the tree, which Module 2 set to one in `rpart()`, and which travels with the fitted tree into `adaboost()`, as the handoff of Module 3 explained. The pruning and leaf-size controls of `rpart()` (`cp = 0.01`, `minbucket = 7`) stay at their defaults throughout. The boosting adds two hyperparameters of its own, the number of rounds and the learning rate, both arguments of `adaboost()`. A grid crosses values of all three. Listing 33 defines one with depths 1 to 3, so stumps and two kinds of shallow trees; 10, 100 and 1,000 rounds; and learning rates of 1 and 0.1. That makes 18 settings. Two expectations guide the choice of values. More rounds call for a smaller learning rate, because at a rate of 1 a long run of rounds overfits noisy data. Deeper trees fit the training data faster and overfit sooner, so they need the same care. The grid is coarse on purpose. On a laptop we prefer small runs and successive refinement to one exhaustive search, and the package ships an exhaustive search below. The rows of the grid also store the results: one column per tuning project for the AUROC of the held-out project, and one for the run time.
:::

#### Listing 33

Code to define a hypergrid.

```{r listing-33}
# The grid: every combination of three hyperparameters
hgrid <- expand.grid(
  # Tree level: the maximum depth
  depth = 1:3,
  # Boosting level: the number of rounds
  n_iter = c(10, 100, 1000),
  # Boosting level: the learning rate
  eta = c(1, 0.1)
)

# Containers: the AUROC per tuning project and the run time per setting
hgrid[proj_nms] <- NA_real_
hgrid$runtime <- NA_real_
```

::: {.callout-important title="Changed since submission"}
- `n_iter` (was `T`), the name the package reads; the comments name the level of each hyperparameter.
- The containers follow `expand.grid()`: one column per tuning project from `proj_nms` of Listing 32, so ML2 is in and HOLZ is out (submitted: five named `NA` columns inside `expand.grid()`, plus `auc.mean`). The summary columns are added in Listing 34, where they are computed.
:::

#### Listing 34

Code to do hyperparameter optimization using leave-one-group-out cross-validation.

```{r listing-34}
# The formula, written out: `.` would pull `pid` in
fml <- replicate ~ power.o + effect_size.o + n.o + p_value.o

# Hyperparameter optimization: one LOGO-CV per setting
for (i in seq_len(nrow(hgrid))) {
  # Progress report, overwritten in place
  cat("\rSetting", i, "of", nrow(hgrid))
  runtime <- system.time({
    # The LOGO-CV of Listing 32 at this setting, by the package function
    logo_i <- logo_cv(
      fml,
      data = df_noholz,
      group = "pid",
      depth = hgrid$depth[i],
      n_iter = hgrid$n_iter[i],
      eta = hgrid$eta[i]
    )
  })
  # The AUROC per held-out project and the run time in seconds
  hgrid[i, proj_nms] <- logo_i$estimates[1, proj_nms, "auroc"]
  hgrid$runtime[i] <- runtime[["elapsed"]]
}

# Stability: the mean across projects minus their SD
proj_auc <- as.matrix(hgrid[proj_nms])
hgrid$auc_mean <- rowMeans(proj_auc)
hgrid$auc_sd <- apply(proj_auc, 1, sd)
hgrid$auc_stable <- hgrid$auc_mean - hgrid$auc_sd

# The grid, most stable setting first
hgrid[order(-hgrid$auc_stable), ] |> round(2)
```

::: {.callout-note title="Add to tutorial"}
Listing 34 wraps one loop around the cross-validation of Module 6. The loop visits each row of the grid, and the call inside it is the LOGO-CV of Listing 32 at that row's setting, done by the package function: `logo_cv()` takes the formula, the data with their project column, and the setting as `depth`, `n_iter` and `eta`. Readers who stayed by hand paste the loop of Listing 32 in its place and read the setting off the row. The result holds the AUROC of every held-out project, which the loop copies into the row together with the run time. The progress report uses a carriage return, so `cat()` overwrites one line instead of printing 18. After the loop, three columns summarize each row: the mean AUROC across the six projects, their standard deviation, and the difference of the two, which we call *stability*. The mean alone would favor a setting that excels on three projects and fails on the other three; the mean minus the SD favors a setting that does well everywhere. Stability is a ranking device, not a performance estimate. Module 6 explained why six unequal and overlapping folds give no honest mean with a standard error, and nothing here reports one.

**A Fourth Look at Performance.** The most stable of the 18 settings is a stump boosted for 1,000 rounds at a learning rate of 0.1 (stability 0.66; mean 0.78, SD 0.12). Its worst project is ML3 at 0.64, its best ML1 at 0.96. The ensemble of Module 3, the same stump for 1,000 rounds at a rate of 1, is the least stable of all (0.54): on ML3 it ranks below chance (0.48). At many rounds, the learning rate has to come down. Ten rounds at a rate of 1 come close to the top (0.64 for depth 2, 0.63 for the stump), so the cheapest settings of the grid are nearly as good as its best. Deeper trees buy nothing here: at a rate of 0.1, depth 2 and 3 rank below depth 1 at every number of rounds, and at a rate of 1 the three depths trade places near the bottom. The run time shows the cost: 20 to 25 s for 1,000 rounds against less than half a second for 10. In short, a stump at a low learning rate is the safe choice on this grid, but the differences among the top settings are smaller than six projects can resolve.
:::

## Random Search

::: {.callout-note title="Add to tutorial"}
A grid grows fast. Three depths, three round counts and two rates make 18 settings, and the grid of the next section has 2,640. A random search draws a sample of settings instead of visiting all of them. For a fixed budget of fits it often finds a setting as good as the grid's best, because a grid spends its budget evenly, including on hyperparameters that matter little. Listing [NEW] draws eight of the 18 settings and hands them to `logo_cv()`, which scores them as before; the seed makes the draw reproducible. The run time is the budget: the eight settings took about 68 s against about 2.5 minutes for the full grid. The draw found the grid's second-best setting, the stump with 100 rounds at a rate of 0.1 (stability 0.64), and missed the best (0.66). On a grid this small, the random search is a demonstration. It becomes the tool of choice when a full grid would run for hours, and it combines with refinement: draw first, then refine the grid around the best draws.
:::

#### Listing [NEW]

Code to do a random search over the hypergrid.

```{r listing-random}
# Draw eight settings from the grid instead of trying all 18
set.seed(112)
hgrid_rnd <- hgrid[sample(nrow(hgrid), 8), c("depth", "n_iter", "eta")]

# Score the drawn settings by LOGO-CV, as in Listing 34
runtime_rnd <- system.time({
  logo_rnd <- logo_cv(fml, data = df_noholz, group = "pid", grid = hgrid_rnd)
})
runtime_rnd[["elapsed"]]

# Stability of the drawn settings, most stable first
auc_rnd <- logo_rnd$estimates[, proj_nms, "auroc"]
hgrid_rnd$auc_stable <- rowMeans(auc_rnd) - apply(auc_rnd, 1, sd)
hgrid_rnd[order(-hgrid_rnd$auc_stable), ] |> round(2)
```

## A Larger Grid

::: {.callout-note title="Add to tutorial"}
Listing 34 searched 18 settings in about 2.5 minutes. The package ships a much larger search as the dataset `hypergrid`: 2,640 settings, with depths 1 to 8, 15 learning rates from 0.0025 to 1, and 10 to 3,000 rounds, each scored by LOGO-CV on the same six tuning projects under all 17 measures of `assess()`. HOLZ took no part, so it stays untouched for the final test. `hypergrid` is a list with one table per measure. In each table a row is a setting and a column a project, with no summaries, because the summary is the modeler's decision. Listing [NEW] loads it and adds the summary of Listing 34 plus one more column, the worst project of each setting.

Before ranking, look at the projects one by one. Over all 2,640 settings, the median AUROC is 0.93 on ML1 but 0.64 on ML3 and RPP, and RPP, the largest project with 90 study effects, never gets above 0.69. The projects differ far more than the settings do. This repeats Module 6's finding at scale: no setting makes RPP easy, and almost every setting makes ML1 look good.
:::

#### Listing [NEW]

Code to load the hypergrid of the adatutor package and summarize it.

```{r hypergrid-load}
# The shipped search: a table per measure, a row per setting, a column per
# project
data(hypergrid)
names(hypergrid)
auc_all <- hypergrid$auroc
proj_nms <- attr(hypergrid, "projects")$project

# The projects one by one: the median AUROC over all settings
proj_all <- as.matrix(auc_all[proj_nms])
apply(proj_all, 2, median) |> round(2)

# Stability as in Listing 34, and the worst project
auc_all$auc_mean <- rowMeans(proj_all)
auc_all$auc_sd <- apply(proj_all, 1, sd)
auc_all$auc_stable <- auc_all$auc_mean - auc_all$auc_sd
auc_all$auc_min <- apply(proj_all, 1, min)
```

::: {.callout-important title="Changed since submission"}
- New listing: `hypergrid` is new in the package (R1.C2 asked for more than "a grid that runs fast").
:::

#### Listing [NEW]

Code to choose a setting from the hypergrid.

```{r hypergrid-pick}
# All settings, most stable first
ranked <- auc_all[order(-auc_all$auc_stable, -auc_all$auc_min), ]
cols <- c("depth", "n_iter", "eta", proj_nms, "auc_stable", "auc_min")
head(ranked[cols], 3) |> print(digits = 2, row.names = FALSE)

# The most stable stump
best_d1 <- ranked[ranked$depth == 1, ][1, ]

# Settings no other setting beats on both counts: down the list, keep a row
# only if its worst project beats every row above it
unbeaten <- ranked[
  ranked$auc_min > cummax(c(-Inf, head(ranked$auc_min, -1))),
]
rbind(best_d1, unbeaten)[cols] |> print(digits = 2, row.names = FALSE)

# The choice: the best worst project, ties by stability
best <- auc_all[order(-auc_all$auc_min, -auc_all$auc_stable), ][1, ]
best[c("depth", "n_iter", "eta", "auc_stable", "auc_min")]
```

::: {.callout-note title="Add to tutorial"}
The most stable setting of all is a tree of depth 5, boosted for 40 rounds at a rate of 0.02 (stability 0.69, worst project 0.66). The most stable stump, 200 rounds at a rate of 0.5, is close behind (0.67, worst project 0.67). Stability is not the only thing we care about, though. The final test of Module 8 is a single new project, so what a setting does on its worst project counts as much as its average. Only three settings are unbeaten on both counts, with no other setting both more stable and better on its worst project: the depth-5 trees, a depth-6 tree with 30 rounds at a rate of 0.03, and a depth-2 tree with 2,000 rounds at a rate of 0.02. Their stabilities are almost on par, within 0.02 of each other, but the depth-2 tree has the best worst project, 0.68 against 0.66 and 0.67. So despite the slightly higher stability of the depth-5 trees, we choose the depth-2 tree with 2,000 rounds at a rate of 0.02. It boosts a weak learner in many small steps, as AdaBoost intends, and it sits on a plateau: its worst project stays between 0.66 and 0.68 from 800 to 2,500 rounds. The last lines of Listing [NEW] make the rule explicit, the best worst project with ties broken by stability, and store the choice in `best`, which Module 8 refits. All three would have been a good choice: they differ by less than 0.02 on either measure, well within what six projects can resolve. One table of `hypergrid` has gaps: precision among the top five is undefined for ML3, which has three successes (`?hypergrid`).
:::

# Module 8: Finalizing an Ensemble / Final Tests and Benchmarks

#### Listing 35

Code to refit the safeguard setting of the hypergrid on the six tuning projects
and test it on HOLZ.

```{r listing-35}
# The safeguard setting from the hypergrid: depth 2, n_iter 2000, eta .02
best[c("depth", "n_iter", "eta")]

# Refit it on all six tuning projects
h_final <- rpart::rpart(
  replicate ~ .,
  data = df_noholz[, voi_nms],
  maxdepth = best$depth,
  model = TRUE
)
fit_final <- adaboost(h_final, n_iter = best$n_iter, eta = best$eta)

# The final test: score it once on HOLZ, on the margin so the AUC sees the
# ranking
y_ada <- predict(fit_final, newdata = df_holz[, pred_nms], type = "margin")
auroc(df_holz$replicate, y_ada)
```

## Selecting versus Evaluating

Listing 34 scores every setting in the hypergrid on the six tuning projects, and we took the row with the most stable performance. I think that this number is not an estimate of how the chosen model will do on a new project, because the same six projects picked the winner and then graded it. To see how much that matters, we should do the selection where the project we want to score cannot influence it.
