## Addition: Nested LOGO-CV

Setting a project aside costs data: HOLZ's 26 studies never helped choose the
setting, and the final test in Listing 35 rests on those 26 studies alone.
Nested LOGO-CV avoids both. It repeats the whole procedure -- search the grid,
pick the winner, refit it -- once per project, each time with that project held
out. Every project serves as the test once, and none is withheld from tuning for
good. The result estimates the procedure, not any single setting, and it shows
which setting each search chose, so you see how stable the choice is. It is
worth its cost, one grid search per project, when the data are too few to spare
a test project, or when the stability of the choice is itself the question.

::: {.callout-note}
## Nested LOGO-CV picks by the mean

`logo_cv(nested = TRUE)` lets each inner search pick the setting with the
highest mean AUROC (`criterion = "auroc"`), not the highest mean minus SD that
Listing 34 uses. Listing 36 ranks by the mean as well, so its two versions agree
with each other, but not with the stability rule of the main thread. To nest
that rule, rank the inner settings by mean minus SD inside the loop of
Listing 36.
:::

In nested leave-one-group-out cross-validation, the outer loop holds
out one project entirely and the inner loop repeats the whole grid search on the six that remain, choosing hyperparameters without ever seeing the held-out project. The
chosen setting is then refit on those six projects and scored on the seventh.
Repeat seven times.

When I first met Nested LOGO-CV, I had a hard time to wrap my head around the fact, that it does not give me a(n overall) performance estimate for a particular hyperparameter setting. 
Instead, it puts a number (an estimate) on the procedure: "run the grid search, pick, then fit the winner." Every model built inside the nesting is discarded; none of them is the model you ship. You still fit one setting on all the projects you have. Nesting tells you what to expect from that
model, not what it scores.

completely separating the tuning process from the evaluation process

if you have a very large training validation and test set you can do the tripple, but if you have very vew data (as we comparably do) we might consider moving to nested cross-validation.

Take our data and split it into folds (the 5 groups in our case). Then we reserve one group, say Group 1, as test set (let's call this the outer test set). 
Then we take the remaining 4 (Group 2, 3, 4, 5) and split them again into 4 pieces: 3 pieces (Group 2, 3, 4) for the training set and one for the (inner) test set (Group 5). Then we (randomly, we do full Cartesian) search a hyperparameter setting from our test set and train the model with the inner 3 pieces (Group 2, 3, 4) and score it on the inner test set (Group 5) - and then again with a different hyperparameter setting. Then, we select the winning model with the best hyperparameter combi on Group 5 and pass it to the outer loop and train the model using the bigger training set with 4 pieces (Group 2, 3, 4, 5) and then evaluate it on the outer test set (Group 1). And then you repeat the whole procedure again with the next group
So instead of one model performance on on test set we have 5 (5 Groups) measures. What people than usually do is to take the mean performance across projects.
So we use all the data as a test set once

In small test set you can have the problem of bad luck and up (especially with small test sets) with a handy partition which is too easy to classify and (thus not representative of what would usually happen, i.e. performane overestimate).

TODO: Random grid search. Define 20 as a number in the random search

Two things follow. First, the seven inner searches may each select a different
setting, and the setting that won in Listing 34 may be chosen by none of them.
That is expected rather than alarming: with seven projects there is no stable
"best" setting to find, and seeing that instability directly is more informative
than the average that hides it. Second, the nested estimate is *conservative*
here, because each nested model saw six projects while a model fitted on all of
them sees seven.

If nesting does not hand you a model, what does? The three listings have three
different jobs, and it is worth being explicit about which is which:

| job | listing |
|:----|:--------|
| Choose the hyperparameters, using the six tuning projects | Listing 34 |
| Estimate what that choice is worth, on one held-out project | Listing 35 |
| Estimate what the choosing procedure is worth, with every project held out once | Listing 36 |

So Listing 34 still picks the setting and Listing 35 still tests it -- nesting
changes neither. What it adds is a number for the whole procedure: not the
winning score from Listing 34, which the same six projects produced by selecting
it, and not a single test project, but an estimate from every project, none of
which had a hand in choosing its own setting.

The settings the inner searches picked are worth looking at, but they are a
diagnostic rather than a shortlist. They have the same standing as the
coefficients fitted inside each cross-validation fold back in Module 1: nobody
averages those, and nobody asks which fold's coefficients to keep. They are
by-products of a procedure being measured, not candidates for shipping.

#### Listing 36

Code to do a nested leave-one-group-out cross-validation.

::: {.callout-note}
This ran for approximately 10 minutes on our laptops.
:::

```{r listing-36}
# Projects, in the order they take their turn: all seven, HOLZ included
projects <- sort(unique(df$pid))

# Partition data by project ID
df_split <- split(df, df$pid)

# One honest score and one selected setting per project
nested_auc <- list()
selected <- list()

runtime <- system.time({
  # OUTER loop: evaluates
  for (rp in projects) {
    # Progress report
    message("\nOuter fold: ", rp, "\n")

    # Training and test set. The test project leaves the data entirely, so
    # nothing below can see it.
    test <- df_split[[rp]]
    train <- df[!(df$pid %in% rp), ]

    # INNER loop: selects. This is the same grid search as Listing 34, run on
    # the training projects only -- so we can hand it to logo_cv().
    inner <- logo_cv(
      replicate ~ power.o + effect_size.o + n.o + p_value.o,
      data = train,
      group = "pid",
      grid = hgrid[, c("depth", "n_iter", "eta")]
    )

    # Rank the settings by their mean over the inner folds. Here the mean is a
    # ranking device, not a performance estimate.
    inner_auc <- summary(inner, metric = "auroc")
    ranked <- aggregate(estimate ~ setting, data = inner_auc, FUN = mean)

    # The setting the six training projects chose, on their own
    inner_best <- hgrid[ranked$setting[which.max(ranked$estimate)], ]
    selected[[rp]] <- inner_best[, c("depth", "n_iter", "eta")]

    # Refit at that setting and score the untouched project
    h <- rpart::rpart(
      replicate ~ .,
      data = train[, voi_nms],
      maxdepth = inner_best$depth,
      model = TRUE
    )
    fit <- adaboost(
      h,
      n_iter = inner_best$n_iter,
      eta = inner_best$eta,
      verbose = FALSE
    )
    y_pred <- predict(
      fit,
      newdata = test[, pred_nms],
      type = "margin",
      verbose = FALSE
    )
    nested_auc[[rp]] <- auroc(test$replicate, y_pred)
  }
})

# Waiting time
message("Run time: ", runtime["elapsed"], " s\n")

# The honest expectation, per project
unlist(nested_auc)

# What each outer fold selected, and how often they disagree
do.call(rbind, selected)
```

Only the outer loop is new. The inner one is the leave-one-group-out search we
already ran in Listing 34, so we hand it to `logo_cv()` rather than write it out
again -- the single change is that it now sees `train` instead of `df_noholz`.

The whole procedure is also one call:

```{r listing-36-oneline}
nested <- logo_cv(
  replicate ~ power.o + effect_size.o + n.o + p_value.o,
  data = df,
  group = "pid",
  grid = hgrid[, c("depth", "n_iter", "eta")],
  nested = TRUE,
  criterion = "auroc"
)
nested
```

# Conclusion

::: {.callout-note title="Add to tutorial"}
AdaBoost is also the simplest member of the boosting family that applied work uses today. Friedman et al. [-@friedman2000] showed that AdaBoost fits an additive model one stump at a time, and that each round minimizes an exponential loss: the observation weights of Module 3 are, up to a sign, the gradient of that loss. Replacing the exponential loss by the log loss gives LogitBoost, which returns probabilities instead of margins. Replacing the reweighting by a gradient step on any differentiable loss gives gradient boosting [@friedman2001], the algorithm behind XGBoost [@chen2016]. Readers who built AdaBoost by hand in Module 3 have therefore built the skeleton of all of them: a weak learner, T rounds, a learning rate, and a loss that decides what the next round corrects.
:::
